title: Euclid’s view of spiral galaxy NGC 6744
caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 6744, imaged by ESA’s Euclid space telescope
celestial: NGC 6744 · constellation Pavo · about 30 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, image processing by J.-C. Cuillandre (CEA Paris-Saclay), G. Anselmi

recognition.text: Part of Euclid’s Early Release Observations, May 2024 (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: The whole of the spiral galaxy NGC 6744 fits inside this single Euclid frame, from its broad arms down to fine lanes of dust. Feathery “spurs” of dust branch off the spiral arms. The galaxy lies about 30 million light-years away in Pavo, the Peacock.

NGC 6744 is one of the largest spiral galaxies beyond our local neighborhood, and a textbook example of the kind of galaxy that forms most of the stars in the nearby universe. Spiral arms compress gas as they move, so most new stars form along them, yet exactly how spirals drive star formation is still not fully understood.

Spurs like these can only form in a strong enough spiral, which makes them useful clues. With this data, astronomers can count individual stars, map stars and dust, look for globular clusters, and search for dwarf galaxies. Euclid has already found a new dwarf satellite of NGC 6744, despite how closely it has been studied.
scale: Using the source’s listed field of view (41 × 41 arcminutes) and the source’s distance of about 30 million light-years, the frame spans roughly 360,000 × 360,000 light-years. Its light set out about 30 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Euclid combined its visible-light camera (VIS) with near-infrared measurements in the Y and H bands from its NISP instrument. Blue shows light at about 0.7 microns, green about 1.1 microns and red about 1.7 microns.
understand.eye: Two of the three colors are near-infrared light, invisible to the eye, and the mapping was chosen for looks: hot stars read white-blue and dusty regions red.

explore: The image comes from about an hour of observing. The six spikes on bright stars come from diffraction in Euclid’s optics, and a few faint, fuzzy blue circles are “optical ghosts,” ordinary artifacts of a complex optical system that don’t affect the science.
